publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Optical Multiple Access Networks

articleTitle: Passive signalling in optical fibre multiple access networks
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Optical Multiple Access Networks
abstract: In a conventional optical fibre network, whether loop, ring, tree or star, a receiver and an optical source are normally provided at each terminal. However, there are a number of situations in which a multiplicity of active sources is unnecessary or uneconomic, or possibly even leads to degraded performance of the network. The paper summarises how one or two optical sources can be shared by many users in various configurations of multiple access networks.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Optical switching with directional coupler switches and delay lines
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Optical Multiple Access Networks
abstract: Optical time-division multiplexing is a technique that is suitable for future ultrafast optical communications networks. The paper describes some theoretical results on switching architectures which are equivalent to TST networks. They are constructed from 2*2 switches and delay lines. Here, implementation with lithium niobate switches and fibre delay lines is assumed, although other technologies could be used. The use of delay line memories allows block multiplexing to be used, where a block of several bits is held in each timeslot. A guard band between blocks allows each directional coupler switch to change state between timeslots. Also, delay lines imply bit-rate and coding format transparency.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A field demonstration of wavelength routed optical networks
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Optical Multiple Access Networks
abstract: These experimental demonstrations have taken wavelength routing from the laboratory into British Telecom's (BT's) London Main Optical Fibre Network. It shows the ability of this technique to form effective transparent optical networks. Components and sub-assemblies that are available commercially have been used throughout to emphasise the practicality of constructing the networks without the use of state of the art technology. The significant multiplexing and demultiplexing losses at the network nodes limit the range of basic wavelength routed networks. However, this demonstration has shown that useful ranges of up to 40 km for 622 Mbit/s data can be achieved even without amplification. With optical amplification, large networks are possible and in this demonstration amplification allowed transmission lengths of 88.8 km to be demonstrated for the 622 Mbit/s signals. This was achieved with an optical power margin of 12 dB. This distance corresponds to twice the diameter of the existing London Main Fibre Network.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Passive optical multi-access networks for telecommunications
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Optical Multiple Access Networks
abstract: Passive optical networks (PONs) are the most effective way of delivering narrowband services to customers via fibre. PONs also provide an evolutionary path to the delivery of future broadband services. The paper outlines the present stage of development of PONs for use in British Telecom's access network and describes PON architectures for delivering services to both business and residential customers. The upgrade options for providing future broadband services are discussed, and the technology trial at Bishop's Stortford is described.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Wavelength and time switching using semiconductor nonlinear optical amplifiers
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Optical Multiple Access Networks
abstract: The role of optical switching within transparent optical transmission networks is discussed. Particular attention is paid to the need for wavelength switches within wavelength routed optical networks. A wavelength switch based on the absorptive nonlinearity within multi-contact semiconductor optical amplifiers is described. The authors demonstrate wavelength conversion of 400 Mbit/s data between 1.3 mu m and a wavelength over a 30 nm range centered on 1.55 mu m. This shows the suitability of such a device for linking the present 1.3 mu m network to future 1.55 mu m wavelength networks.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Fast synchronous switching in an optical time-multiplexed space switch (OPTIMUSS)
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Optical Multiple Access Networks
abstract: The authors have demonstrated the principle of a fast optical time-space-time switch capable of expansion to capacities in the order of terabits per second. The (sparsely populated) 16*16, strictly nonblocking switch breaks into an SDH bit stream and operate synchronously with it. The overall switch structure is polarisation independent but incorporates polarisation scrambling techniques in conjunction with polarisation sensitive 1:16 hybrid Mach-Zehnder switches. These lithium niobate components have been realised with fibre to fibre losses as low as 7.5 dB and extinction ratios of better than 25 dB. Polarisation sensitivity is traded, in the active part of the switch, for a low switching voltage of less than 6 V. Together with hybrid packaging of synchronisation and drive electronics, this enables transition times of under 5 ns to be achieved. The switch is capable of routing STM or ATM packets as short as 12.9 ns without significant degradation, regardless of the bit rate or number of wavelengths channels (within a 50 nm window) carried.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: System performance of a wavelength division multiplexed source using a multichannel grating cavity laser
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Optical Multiple Access Networks
abstract: Reports on investigations to determine the performance of a recently developed multichannel grating cavity (MGC) laser for use in wavelength division multiplexed (WDM) systems with large spectral separations between channels. Depending upon the application, the MGC laser can operate either as a wavelength switchable source or as a device able to generate multiple spectral channels simultaneously. The laser allows wavelength switching between channels across the entire laser gain spectrum and is designed to allow a large spectral channel separation (>1 nm) with the potential for stable narrow linewidth monomode operation. Particular emphasis is given to channel crosstalk reduction and spectral switching times as low as 2 ns are reported.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Acousto-optic tunable filters for wavelength division multiplexed optical fibre systems
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Optical Multiple Access Networks
abstract: The three important device elements of a channel selecting lithium niobate acousto-optic tunable filter (operating at both 1.3 mu m and 1.55 mu m) are the optical waveguide, the surface acoustic wave (SAW) transducer and the waveguide polariser. The design and fabrication of these elements to achieve low loss, broad tunability and narrow passband are reported and the performance of a channel selecting filter when fully packaged with fibre tails and components for temperature control is described.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: An optoelectronic sampling receiver for time-division multiple access network applications
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Optical Multiple Access Networks
abstract: A new receiver for time division multiple access (TDMA) network applications is described, which uses a InGaAs/InP PIN diode as an optoelectronic sampling gate. Error-free sampling of 2 Mbit/s data from a 64 Mbit/s 1.3 mu m optical data stream at -23.5 dBm has been achieved. An in-band technique for timing signal provision is proposed and demonstrated.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: High density wavelength division multiplexing for multiple access networks
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Optical Multiple Access Networks
abstract: High density wavelength multiplexing within a passive optical interconnect allows multiple connections independent of bit rate and data format, providing service transparency and a high level of flexibility. A number of optical filtering technologies are available for channel access or selection. For WDM channels spaced in the 1 to 5 nm band using DFB lasers, interference filters or grating based demultiplexers provide the required performance for selectivity, crosstalk and insertion loss. The authors demonstrated a novel implementation of a grating demultiplexer in the form of a multichannel grating demultiplexer (MGD) receiver where a high (>60%) channel width/spacing ratio is achieved by the choice of detector dimensions.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A lithium niobate digital optical waveguide switch for optical circuit protection
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Optical Multiple Access Networks
abstract: Electro-optic waveguide switches are capable of switching at very high speeds and by careful design broadband optical switches which are insensitive to polarisation can be produced that are compatible with existing fibre optic networks. The design and fabrication of a polarisation independent lithium niobate digital optical switch and its performance at both 1.3 mu m and 1.5 mu m is reported. The performance of this device when operated as a protection switch in a 140 Mbit/s wavelength multiplexed optical fibre system is described and the implications for optical network design if switches of this type were to be employed is considered.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A multichannel strategy for high traffic throughput local area networks using wavelength division multiplexing
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Optical Multiple Access Networks
abstract: Addresses the requirement of local area networks (LAN) to maintain performance under asymmetric traffic loads and hence to operate effectively with diverse service requirements. Current research centres on the performance of a multichannel architecture utilising attempt and defer protocols. The advantages of adopting a multichannel architecture on an optical fibre LAN are discussed. The network performance was investigated via discrete event simulation and the results are presented in the form of mean delay/throughput characteristics. The network transmission rates were investigated at 500 Mbit/s and 1 Gbit/s.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>
